question: According to the Rhode Island CDL manual, what is the school bus "danger zone"?
choice_a: The area on all sides of the bus where children are in the most danger of being hit, either by another vehicle or their own bus
choice_b: The area covered only by the interior rearview mirror
choice_c: The zone where the ABS malfunction lamp is visible
choice_d: The area behind the bus that is monitored only by the convex mirrors
explanation: The manual defines the danger zone as the area on all sides of the bus where children are in the most danger of being hit, either by another vehicle or their own bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: How far can the danger zone extend from the front bumper of a school bus?
choice_a: 10 feet
choice_b: 20 feet
choice_c: As much as 30 feet
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: The manual states the danger zones may extend as much as 30 feet from the front bumper.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: Of the danger zone extending up to 30 feet in front of the bus, which portion is considered the most dangerous?
choice_a: The last 10 feet, closest to where students board
choice_b: The middle 10 feet
choice_c: The entire 30 feet equally
choice_d: The first 10 feet
explanation: The manual specifies that of the danger zone extending up to 30 feet from the front bumper, the first 10 feet is the most dangerous.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: How far do the danger zones extend from the left and right sides of the school bus, and from behind the rear bumper?
choice_a: 5 feet on each side and behind
choice_b: 10 feet
choice_c: 15 feet
choice_d: 25 feet
explanation: The manual states the danger zones extend 10 feet from the left and right sides of the bus and 10 feet behind the rear bumper.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: Why is the area to the left of the school bus always considered dangerous, according to the manual?
choice_a: Because of passing cars
choice_b: Because the fuel tank is located there
choice_c: Because the crossover mirror does not cover that side
choice_d: Because the stop signal arm is mounted there
explanation: The manual states that the area to the left of the bus is always considered dangerous because of passing cars.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.1 Danger Zones

question: When should a school bus driver check each mirror to obtain maximum viewing area?
choice_a: Only at the end of the route
choice_b: Only when a student reports a problem
choice_c: Always before operating the school bus
choice_d: Only once per week
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to always check each mirror before operating the school bus to obtain maximum viewing area, and to have the mirrors adjusted if necessary.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.2 Correct Mirror Adjustment

question: What is the purpose of the outside left and right side flat mirrors?
choice_a: To monitor passenger activity inside the bus
choice_b: To view only the engine compartment
choice_c: To monitor traffic, check clearances, and see students on the sides and to the rear of the bus
choice_d: To indicate ABS malfunctions
explanation: The manual states the flat mirrors are used to monitor traffic, check clearances and students on the sides and to the rear of the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.3 Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: Where is a blind spot located relative to the outside flat mirrors, besides directly behind the rear bumper?
choice_a: Immediately below and in front of each mirror
choice_b: Directly above the windshield
choice_c: Inside the passenger compartment only
choice_d: At the front bumper danger zone only
explanation: The manual notes there is a blind spot immediately below and in front of each flat mirror, and directly in back of the rear bumper.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.3 Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: According to the manual, how far behind the bus does the blind spot typically extend, and how far could it extend depending on the length and width of the bus?
choice_a: 5 to 10 feet, could extend to 50 feet
choice_b: It never extends more than 100 feet
choice_c: 100 to 200 feet, could extend up to 500 feet
choice_d: 50 to 150 feet, could extend up to 400 feet
explanation: The manual states the blind spot behind the bus extends 50 to 150 feet and could extend up to 400 feet depending on the length and width of the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.3 Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: When properly adjusted, how far behind the bus should the outside flat mirrors allow the driver to see?
choice_a: 100 feet or 2 bus lengths
choice_b: 150 feet or 3 bus lengths
choice_c: 200 feet or 4 bus lengths
choice_d: 300 feet or 6 bus lengths
explanation: The manual states properly adjusted flat mirrors should allow the driver to see 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.3 Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: Where are the outside left and right side convex mirrors located on a school bus?
choice_a: Below the outside flat mirrors
choice_b: Above the outside flat mirrors
choice_c: On the rear emergency door
choice_d: Directly above the windshield
explanation: The manual states the convex mirrors are located below the outside flat mirrors.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.4 Outside Left and Right Side Convex Mirrors

question: What is a key limitation of the outside convex mirrors noted in the manual?
choice_a: They cannot be adjusted
choice_b: They only work at night
choice_c: They only show the interior of the bus
choice_d: They present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus
explanation: The manual warns that convex mirrors present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.4 Outside Left and Right Side Convex Mirrors

question: When properly positioned, what should the outside convex mirrors allow the driver to see along the side of the bus?
choice_a: The entire side of the bus up to the mirror mounts
choice_b: Only the rear bumper
choice_c: Only the front bumper
choice_d: The engine compartment
explanation: The manual states convex mirrors should be positioned to see the entire side of the bus up to the mirror mounts.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.4 Outside Left and Right Side Convex Mirrors

question: Where are the outside left and right side crossover mirrors mounted on a school bus?
choice_a: On both left and right front corners of the bus
choice_b: On the rear emergency door
choice_c: Below the convex mirrors
choice_d: Inside the bus above the driver
explanation: The manual states crossover mirrors are mounted on both left and right front corners of the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.5 Outside Left and Right Side Crossover Mirrors

question: What is the crossover mirrors' purpose in relation to the front bumper danger zone?
choice_a: They amplify sound near the front bumper
choice_b: They are used to see the front bumper danger zone area directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision
choice_c: They only display warning lights
choice_d: They are used exclusively at railroad crossings
explanation: The manual states crossover mirrors are used to see the front bumper danger zone area directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.5 Outside Left and Right Side Crossover Mirrors

question: When properly adjusted, the crossover mirrors should show the entire area in front of the bus from the front bumper at ground level to a point where direct vision is possible. What should happen between direct vision and mirror view vision?
choice_a: They should never overlap
choice_b: Only direct vision should be used
choice_c: Only mirror vision should be used
choice_d: They should overlap
explanation: The manual states direct vision and mirror view vision should overlap.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.5 Outside Left and Right Side Crossover Mirrors

question: Where is the overhead inside rearview mirror mounted, and what is its primary use?
choice_a: Mounted above the windshield on the driver's side, used to monitor passenger activity inside the bus
choice_b: Mounted on the rear bumper, used to monitor traffic behind the bus
choice_c: Mounted at the front corners, used to check tire clearance
choice_d: Mounted on the service door, used to check student boarding
explanation: The manual states the overhead inside rearview mirror is mounted directly above the windshield on the driver's side area and is used to monitor passenger activity inside the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.6 Overhead Inside Rearview Mirror

question: Besides a blind spot directly behind the driver's seat, what other large blind spot area is associated with the overhead inside rearview mirror, and how far can it extend?
choice_a: There is no additional blind spot
choice_b: A blind spot beginning at the windshield extending 10 feet
choice_c: A blind spot only at the front bumper
choice_d: A blind spot beginning at the rear bumper that could extend up to 400 feet or more
explanation: The manual states there is a large blind spot area that begins at the rear bumper and could extend up to 400 feet or more behind the bus, requiring use of the exterior side mirrors to monitor that area.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.6 Overhead Inside Rearview Mirror

question: When properly positioned, what should appear at the top of the overhead inside rearview mirror?
choice_a: The stop signal arm
choice_b: The service door
choice_c: The top of the rear window
choice_d: The front bumper
explanation: The manual states you should position the overhead mirror to see the top of the rear window in the top of the mirror.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.1.6 Overhead Inside Rearview Mirror

question: According to the manual, which is true about student deaths related to school buses?
choice_a: More students are killed while getting on or off a school bus each year than are killed as passengers inside the bus
choice_b: More students are killed as passengers inside the bus than while getting on or off
choice_c: Student deaths occur equally while boarding and while riding
choice_d: The manual does not address student fatality statistics
explanation: The manual states more students are killed while getting on or off a school bus each year than are killed as passengers inside of a school bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2 Loading and Unloading

question: If the bus is so equipped, when should the driver activate alternating flashing amber warning lights when approaching a stop?
choice_a: At least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law
choice_b: Only after the bus has fully stopped
choice_c: At least 500 feet before the stop
choice_d: Only when students are visible at the stop
explanation: The manual states to activate alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: When approaching a stop, when should the driver turn on the right turn signal indicator?
choice_a: Immediately upon leaving the previous stop
choice_b: At the exact moment the bus stops
choice_c: About 100-300 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds before pulling over
choice_d: Only after the stop arm is extended
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to turn on the right turn signal indicator about 100-300 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds before pulling over.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: How far away from students at the designated stop should the driver bring the school bus to a full stop, and why?
choice_a: At least 5 feet away, so the driver can quickly close the door
choice_b: At least 10 feet away, which forces the students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements
choice_c: At least 25 feet away, to allow more braking distance
choice_d: Right next to the students, to save time
explanation: The manual states the driver should bring the bus to a full stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet away from students at the designated stop, forcing students to walk to the bus for a better view of their movements.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: Before completely opening the door and signaling students to approach, what final check should the driver make?
choice_a: Check that the fuel gauge is above half
choice_b: Check that the dome light is off
choice_c: Check that the radio is functioning
choice_d: Check that all traffic has stopped
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to make a final check to see that all traffic has stopped before completely opening the door and signaling students to approach.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.1 Approaching the Stop

question: According to loading procedures, when should students board the school bus?
choice_a: As soon as the bus arrives at the stop
choice_b: Only when signaled by the driver
choice_c: When the alternating amber lights turn off
choice_d: Whenever they see the stop arm extended
explanation: The manual states students should board the bus only when signaled by the driver, after waiting at a designated location facing the bus as it approaches.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.2 Loading Procedures

question: How should students board the school bus, and what should be on while loading in the dark?
choice_a: Quickly in any order; the headlights should be on
choice_b: Slowly, in single file, using the handrail; the dome light should be on
choice_c: In pairs, without the handrail; the hazard lights should be on
choice_d: In any manner the driver prefers; no lights are needed
explanation: The manual states students should board the bus slowly, in single file, using the handrail, and the dome light should be on while loading in the dark.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.2 Loading Procedures

question: If the driver cannot account for a student outside the bus during loading, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Drive slowly around the block to look
choice_b: Call the next stop to ask if the student is there
choice_c: Wait exactly five minutes then depart
choice_d: Secure the bus, take the key, and check around and underneath the bus
explanation: The manual instructs that if you cannot account for a student outside, secure the bus, take the key, and check around and underneath the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.2 Loading Procedures

question: When students are loading at the school campus, what should the driver do regarding the ignition and key in addition to positioning to supervise loading?
choice_a: Leave the engine running and keep the key in the ignition at all times
choice_b: Turn off the ignition switch and remove the key if leaving the driver's compartment
choice_c: Leave the parking brake off to allow quick departure
choice_d: Turn on the strobe light only
explanation: The manual states that when loading at the school campus, the driver should turn off the ignition switch and remove the key if leaving the driver's compartment, and position to supervise loading as required.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.2 Loading Procedures

question: During unloading on the route, why should the driver count the number of students while unloading?
choice_a: To confirm the location of all students before pulling away from the stop
choice_b: To calculate fuel usage
choice_c: To report attendance to the school office in real time
choice_d: It is not necessary to count students during unloading
explanation: The manual states the driver should count the number of students while unloading to confirm the location of all students before pulling away from the stop.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.3 Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: How far should students be told to walk away from the side of the bus after exiting during unloading on the route?
choice_a: 5 feet
choice_b: At least 10 feet, to a position where the driver can plainly see all students
choice_c: 20 feet
choice_d: There is no specified distance
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to tell students to exit the bus and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can plainly see all students.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.3 Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: If a driver has missed a student's unloading stop, what does the manual say the driver should NOT do?
choice_a: Contact dispatch
choice_b: Continue the route
choice_c: Back up
choice_d: Follow local procedures
explanation: The manual explicitly states that if you have missed a student's unloading stop, do not back up, and to be sure to follow local procedures.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.3 Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: When a student must cross the roadway after exiting the bus, how far should the student walk in front of the right corner of the bumper, while still staying away from the front of the bus?
choice_a: At least 5 feet
choice_b: At least 10 feet
choice_c: At least 25 feet
choice_d: At least 50 feet
explanation: The manual states students should walk to a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, but still remaining away from the front of the school bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.3 Additional Procedures for Students That Must Cross the Roadway

question: Upon the driver's signal to cross, where should students stop and look again before continuing across the roadway?
choice_a: At the right edge of the roadway
choice_b: Halfway across the opposing lane
choice_c: They should not stop again once signaled
choice_d: At the left edge of the school bus
explanation: The manual states students should cross far enough in front of the bus to be in the driver's view, then stop at the left edge of the school bus and look again for the driver's signal to continue crossing.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.3 Additional Procedures for Students That Must Cross the Roadway

question: When unloading at school, what should the driver do after having students exit and before preparing to leave?
choice_a: Immediately drive away once the last student is seen exiting
choice_b: Turn on the interior dome light and leave it on for the rest of the day
choice_c: Only check the fuel level
choice_d: Walk through the bus to check for hiding or sleeping students and items left by students, then check all mirrors
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to walk through the bus and check for hiding/sleeping students and items left by students, then check all mirrors to make certain no students are returning to the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.4 Unloading Procedures at School

question: In the prepare-to-leave steps listed for unloading at school (as opposed to unloading on the route), what additional step involving personal restraint is included before starting the engine?
choice_a: Fastening safety belt
choice_b: Removing shoes
choice_c: Adjusting the seat height
choice_d: No additional step is listed
explanation: The manual's prepare-to-leave steps for unloading at school include closing the door, fastening safety belt, starting the engine, engaging the transmission, and releasing the parking brake, among other steps.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.4 Unloading Procedures at School

topic: Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading
question: If a student drops an object near the bus during loading or unloading, what should students be told to do?
choice_a: Immediately retrieve it themselves, no matter where it landed
choice_b: Leave the object, move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, and try to get the driver's attention to retrieve it
choice_c: Ask another student to retrieve it for them
choice_d: Wait for the bus to move before retrieving it
explanation: The manual states students should be told to leave any dropped object and move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, attempting to get the driver's attention to retrieve the object, since returning for the object could cause a student to disappear from the driver's sight at a dangerous moment.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.5 Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading

topic: Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading
question: What hazard does the manual describe under "Handrail Hang-ups"?
choice_a: Students falling asleep on the bus
choice_b: The handrail rusting and breaking
choice_c: Students being injured or killed when clothing, accessories, or body parts get caught in the handrail or door while exiting
choice_d: Students climbing over the handrail to exit faster
explanation: The manual warns that students have been injured or killed when clothing, accessories, or even parts of their body get caught in the handrail or door as they exited the bus, so the driver should closely observe exiting students before moving.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.5 Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading

question: After a route or school activity trip is finished, what should the driver look for while walking through and around the bus during a post-trip inspection?
choice_a: Only the fuel gauge reading
choice_b: Only the odometer reading
choice_c: Articles left on the bus, sleeping students, open windows and doors, mechanical/operational problems, and damage or vandalism
choice_d: Only tire pressure
explanation: The manual lists articles left on the bus, sleeping students, open windows and doors, mechanical/operational problems (with special attention to mirror systems, flashing warning lamps, and stop signal arms), and damage or vandalism as post-trip inspection items.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.6 Post-trip Inspection

question: What should the driver do if problems or special situations are found during the post-trip inspection?
choice_a: Wait until the next scheduled maintenance to report it
choice_b: Fix the issue personally before the next route
choice_c: Ignore minor issues
choice_d: Report them immediately to the supervisor or school authorities
explanation: The manual states any problems or special situations found should be reported immediately to your supervisor or school authorities.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.2.6 Post-trip Inspection

question: According to the manual's general rule, how is student safety and control best maintained during an emergency or impending crisis?
choice_a: By immediately evacuating in every situation
choice_b: By keeping students on the bus, if doing so does not expose them to unnecessary risk or injury
choice_c: By having students exit through the roof hatch first
choice_d: By calling parents before making any decision
explanation: The manual states that as a general rule, student safety and control is best maintained by keeping students on the bus during an emergency and/or impending crisis situation, if doing so does not expose them to unnecessary risk or injury, but the decision to evacuate must be timely.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.1 Planning for Emergencies

question: Before deciding to evacuate the school bus, what should the driver do if time permits?
choice_a: Contact the dispatcher to explain the situation
choice_b: Wait for a police escort
choice_c: Take a headcount of all students first, regardless of danger
choice_d: Consult the vehicle inspection checklist
explanation: The manual states that if time permits, school bus drivers should contact their dispatcher to explain the situation before making a decision to evacuate the school bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.1 Planning for Emergencies

question: The manual notes that moving students could sometimes complicate certain injuries. Which type of injury does it specifically mention in this context?
choice_a: A sprained ankle
choice_b: A minor bruise
choice_c: A common cold
choice_d: Neck and back injuries and fractures
explanation: The manual lists as a consideration whether moving students would complicate injuries such as neck and back injuries and fractures.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.1 Planning for Emergencies

question: According to the manual, in which of the following situations MUST the driver evacuate the bus?
choice_a: The bus is running five minutes late
choice_b: The bus is stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing
choice_c: A student has a minor disagreement with another student
choice_d: The bus radio is temporarily out of range
explanation: The manual lists mandatory evacuation situations including the bus being on fire or threatened by fire, being stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing, imminent danger of collision, a change in bus position that increases danger, and a need to quickly evacuate due to a hazardous materials spill.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.1 Mandatory Evacuations

question: How far off the road, and in what direction, should a "safe place" generally be located after evacuating a bus?
choice_a: At least 50 feet off the road, behind the bus
choice_b: Directly beside the bus on the shoulder
choice_c: At least 200 feet off the road, downwind of the bus
choice_d: At least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic
explanation: The manual states a safe place will be at least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, to keep students from being hit by debris if another vehicle collides with the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: If there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials, how far upwind should students be led, according to the manual?
choice_a: At least 50 feet
choice_b: At least 100 feet
choice_c: At least 300 feet
choice_d: At least 1,000 feet
explanation: The manual states to lead students upwind of the bus at least 300 feet if there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: If a tornado is sighted in the direct path of the bus and evacuation is ordered, and no building shelter is readily available, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Keep students standing beside the bus
choice_b: Escort students to a nearby ditch or culvert and direct them to lie face down with hands covering their head, far enough away that the bus cannot topple on them
choice_c: Have students remain seated with seatbelts fastened
choice_d: Drive toward the tornado to outrun it
explanation: The manual instructs that if a tornado is sighted and no building shelter is available, students should be escorted to a nearby ditch or culvert, directed to lie face down with hands covering their head, and kept far enough away that the bus cannot topple on them.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: During an evacuation, what should the driver do with a student believed to have suffered a neck or spinal injury?
choice_a: Move the student immediately regardless of the situation
choice_b: Ask another student to carry them off
choice_c: Do not move the student unless his or her life is in immediate danger, and use special procedures to prevent further injury
choice_d: Leave the student on the bus permanently
explanation: The manual states not to move a student believed to have suffered a neck or spinal injury unless his or her life is in immediate danger, and that special procedures must be used to move such victims to prevent further injury.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.3.2 Evacuation Procedures

question: What characterizes a "passive" railroad-highway crossing?
choice_a: It has flashing red lights and gates
choice_b: It does not have any type of traffic control device
choice_c: It is only used by freight trains
choice_d: It requires no stop at all
explanation: The manual defines a passive crossing as one that does not have any type of traffic control device; the driver must stop and the decision to proceed rests entirely in the driver's hands.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.1 Types of Crossings

question: What distinguishes an "active" railroad-highway crossing from a passive one?
choice_a: It has a traffic control device installed to regulate traffic, such as flashing red lights, bells, and/or gates
choice_b: It has no warning signs at all
choice_c: It is only found on multi-lane highways
choice_d: It never requires a stop
explanation: The manual states active crossings have a traffic control device installed at the crossing to regulate traffic, including flashing red lights with or without bells and flashing red lights with bells and gates.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.1 Types of Crossings

question: If there is a white stop line painted on the pavement before railroad tracks, where must the front of the school bus remain while stopped at the crossing?
choice_a: Behind the white stop line
choice_b: On top of the stop line
choice_c: Past the stop line but before the cross-buck sign
choice_d: It does not matter as long as the bus is stopped
explanation: The manual states the front of the school bus must remain behind the white stop line while stopped at the crossing.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices

question: What does a cross-buck sign at a railroad crossing require the driver to do?
choice_a: Turn on the strobe light
choice_b: Proceed without stopping if no train is heard
choice_c: Only slow to half speed
choice_d: Yield the right-of-way to the train
explanation: The manual states the cross-buck sign marks the crossing and requires the driver to yield the right-of-way to the train; if there is no white line painted on the pavement, the driver must stop before the cross-buck sign.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices

question: If the gate at a railroad crossing stays down after the train has passed, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Drive around the gate carefully
choice_b: Honk the horn until the gate rises
choice_c: Do not drive around the gate; instead, call your dispatcher
choice_d: Back the bus away and take an alternate route without reporting it
explanation: The manual instructs that if the gate stays down after the train passes, do not drive around the gate; instead, call your dispatcher.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.2 Warning Signs and Devices

question: When approaching a railroad crossing, approximately how far before the crossing should the driver activate hazard lights to make intentions known?
choice_a: Approximately 50 feet
choice_b: Approximately 100 feet
choice_c: Approximately 200 feet
choice_d: Approximately 500 feet
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to activate hazard lights approximately 200 feet before the crossing to make intentions known.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.3 Recommended Procedures

question: At a railroad crossing, how close and how far may the driver stop from the nearest rail, to have the best view of the tracks?
choice_a: No closer than 5 feet and no farther than 25 feet
choice_b: Exactly 20 feet, no more and no less
choice_c: No closer than 30 feet and no farther than 75 feet
choice_d: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet
explanation: The manual states the driver should stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, where there is the best view of the tracks.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.3 Recommended Procedures

question: As a general rule for determining an acceptable amount of containment or storage area on the far side of a crossing, how many feet should be added to the length of the school bus?
choice_a: 5 feet
choice_b: 10 feet
choice_c: 15 feet
choice_d: 25 feet
explanation: The manual states that as a general rule, you should add 15 feet to the length of the school bus to determine an acceptable amount of containment or storage area.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.3 Recommended Procedures

question: If a school bus stalls or becomes trapped on railroad tracks, what is the immediate priority?
choice_a: Try to restart the engine for at least one minute before evacuating
choice_b: Get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving away at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train
choice_c: Wait for the dispatcher's permission before evacuating
choice_d: Keep students seated with seatbelts fastened
explanation: The manual states that if the bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving everyone far from the bus at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.4 Special Situations

question: At a "passive" crossing where active railroad signals indicate the tracks are clear, what does the manual still require the driver to do?
choice_a: Cross immediately without further checks, since the signals confirm safety
choice_b: Look and listen to be sure it is safe to proceed
choice_c: Wait for a second signal cycle before proceeding
choice_d: Rely solely on the signals since passive crossings have no other markings
explanation: The manual warns to be especially careful at passive crossings: even if there are active railroad signals that indicate the tracks are clear, the driver must look and listen to be sure it is safe to proceed.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.4.4 Special Situations

question: According to the manual, why should a driver avoid dealing with on-bus behavior problems during loading and unloading?
choice_a: Because loading and unloading requires all of the driver's concentration on what is happening outside the bus
choice_b: Because school policy forbids any discipline
choice_c: Because students are never a problem during loading and unloading
choice_d: Because the school administration handles all discipline remotely
explanation: The manual states loading and unloading requires all of the driver's concentration, and the driver should not take their eyes off what is happening outside the bus; behavior problems should wait until unloading students are safely off and moved away.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.5.1 Don't Deal with On-bus Problems When Loading and Unloading

question: Except for school or a designated school bus stop, where may a driver put a student off the bus?
choice_a: At any convenient location along the route
choice_b: At the nearest gas station
choice_c: At a police station only
choice_d: Nowhere else; a student should never be put off the bus except at school or his or her designated school bus stop
explanation: The manual states never to put a student off the bus except at school or at his or her designated school bus stop; if the offense is too serious to safely continue driving, the driver should call for a school administrator or the police.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.5.2 Handling Serious Problems

question: Which vehicles does the Department of Transportation require to have antilock braking systems, according to the manual?
choice_a: Air brake vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998, and hydraulically braked trucks/buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999
choice_b: Only vehicles built after the year 2010
choice_c: Only vehicles with hydraulic brakes regardless of weight
choice_d: All school buses regardless of build date
explanation: The manual states ABS is required on air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998, and hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.6.1 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: In an emergency braking situation on a bus equipped with ABS, what should the driver NOT do?
choice_a: Apply steady braking force
choice_b: Steer around obstacles
choice_c: Pump the brakes
choice_d: Stay in control of the vehicle
explanation: The manual instructs that in emergency braking, the driver should not pump the brakes on a bus with ABS; instead, use only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.6.3 Braking with ABS

question: On older ABS systems, how long could the yellow malfunction lamp stay on at start-up?
choice_a: It never illuminates at start-up
choice_b: Until the vehicle is driven over five mph
choice_c: For exactly one full hour
choice_d: Until the parking brake is released
explanation: The manual states that on older systems, the malfunction lamp could stay on until the vehicle is driving over five mph, whereas on newer vehicles it comes on for a bulb check and then goes out quickly.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.6.4 Braking if ABS is Not Working

question: Which of the following is a true safety reminder about ABS from the manual?
choice_a: ABS allows a driver to follow more closely and drive less carefully
choice_b: ABS will always shorten stopping distance
choice_c: ABS won't prevent skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn
choice_d: ABS increases the vehicle's ultimate stopping power beyond the normal brakes
explanation: The manual states ABS should prevent brake-induced skids but not those caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn (power or turning skids), and clarifies ABS won't necessarily shorten stopping distance, won't increase stopping power, and doesn't permit less careful driving.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.6.5 Safety Reminders

question: When should the overhead white strobe light on an equipped school bus be used?
choice_a: Whenever the bus is loading students
choice_b: Continuously during every trip regardless of conditions
choice_c: Only at railroad crossings
choice_d: When the driver has limited visibility, meaning it is difficult to easily see around the bus in front, behind, or beside it
explanation: The manual states the overhead strobe light should be used when the driver has limited visibility, meaning the driver cannot easily see around the bus, subject to state or local regulations.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.7.1 Strobe Lights

question: The manual compares the side of a school bus in strong winds to what?
choice_a: A sail on a sailboat
choice_b: An anchor
choice_c: A parachute
choice_d: A rudder
explanation: The manual states the side of a school bus acts like a sail on a sailboat, and strong winds can push the bus sideways, move it off the road, or in extreme conditions, tip it over.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.7.2 Driving in High Winds

question: According to the manual, when should a school bus driver back the bus?
choice_a: Only when running behind schedule
choice_b: Whenever convenient to save time
choice_c: Only when there is no other safe way to move the vehicle, and never with students outside the bus
choice_d: Anytime a lookout is available
explanation: The manual states backing a school bus is strongly discouraged and should only be done when there is no other safe way to move the vehicle; a driver should never back a school bus when students are outside of the bus.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.7.3 Backing

question: If no lookout is available when the driver must back the bus, what should the driver do before backing?
choice_a: Back up slowly without any additional precautions
choice_b: Ask a student to serve as the lookout instead
choice_c: Sound the horn twice and proceed immediately
choice_d: Set the parking brake, turn off the motor and take the keys, then walk to the rear of the bus to determine whether the way is clear
explanation: The manual instructs that if no lookout is available, the driver should set the parking brake, turn off the motor and take the keys, and walk to the rear of the bus to determine whether the way is clear.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.7.3 Backing

question: How much tail swing can a school bus have, according to the manual, and what should the driver do to monitor it?
choice_a: Up to one foot; check mirrors only after completing a turn
choice_b: Up to three feet; check mirrors before and during any turning movements
choice_c: Up to six feet; no mirror check is needed
choice_d: Up to ten feet; only a rear lookout can monitor it
explanation: The manual states a school bus can have up to a three-foot tail swing, and the driver needs to check mirrors before and during any turning movements to monitor the tail swing.
source_note: Rhode Island CDL Manual, Section 10 - School Buses, 10.7.4 Tail Swing
